title: WHY DOES SCRIPTURE COMPARE MARITAL LOVE TO INTOXICATION?
paragraphs:
WHY DOES SCRIPTURE COMPARE MARITAL LOVE TO INTOXICATION?
The Bible uses language so intense that it can make religious people uncomfortable—but behind those words is a breathtaking truth about marriage, desire, covenant, and the God who refuses to let sin have the final word.
There is a verse in the Bible that sounds almost dangerous when you first hear it.
Not because it celebrates sin.
Not because God momentarily lowers His standard of holiness.
But because God speaks about marital love with an intensity many Christians have never been taught to expect from Scripture.
“Let her be as the loving hind and pleasant roe; let her breasts satisfy thee at all times; and be thou ravished always with her love.”
That is Proverbs 5:19 in the King James Version.
Read those final words again.
“Be thou ravished always with her love.”
Some modern translations render the thought even more startlingly:
Be intoxicated with her love.
And suddenly we have a question.
Why?

Why would Scripture—a book that repeatedly warns against drunkenness, uncontrolled appetites, adultery, lust, and sexual immorality—borrow the language of intoxication to describe the love between a husband and his wife?
The answer takes us somewhere much deeper than romance.
It takes us into desire.
Into covenant.
Into temptation.
Into the human heart.
And eventually, inevitably, to Jesus Christ.
Because there are desires God does not merely command us to suppress.
There are desires He wants to redeem.
The Hebrew behind Proverbs 5:19 matters.
The final portion reads:
בְּאַהֲבָתָהּ תִּשְׁגֶּה תָמִיד
be’ahavatah tishgeh tamid.
The word אַהֲבָה (ahavah) means “love.”
תָמִיד (tamid) carries the sense of “continually,” “always,” or “regularly.”
But the word that makes the verse unforgettable is תִּשְׁגֶּה (tishgeh), from the Hebrew root שׁגה (shagah).

Depending on context, the verb can carry ideas such as wandering, going astray, being captivated, or being overcome. That is why English translations vary. Some use language such as being “ravished,” others “intoxicated,” others “captivated.”
And context is everything.
Proverbs 5 is not telling a man to lose moral control.
It is warning him not to give his sexuality to another woman.

The chapter is a father’s urgent instruction concerning sexual faithfulness. The forbidden woman initially appears desirable, but the path of adultery leads toward bitterness, loss, regret, and destruction. Then, directly against the counterfeit, Scripture presents the covenant alternative:
“Drink waters out of thine own cistern, and running waters out of thine own well.”
Then:
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Then comes the astonishing command:
Let her satisfy you.
Remain captivated by her.
Be overwhelmed with love for the woman to whom you have given your covenant.
That changes everything.
God is not comparing marital love to sinful drunkenness because drunkenness is good.
He is using vivid language to describe absorption, delight, fascination, and powerful affection within the boundaries of covenant.
In other words:
Don’t become intoxicated with what will destroy you.
Become deeply captivated by the person you promised to love.
That is a word our generation desperately needs.
Because we live in an age that has become extraordinarily skilled at separating desire from covenant.
Swipe.
Watch.
Hide.
Delete the history.
Close the browser.
Send the message.
Erase the message.
Tell yourself it means nothing.
Tell yourself your spouse would not understand.
Tell yourself everybody does it.
Tell yourself you deserve this because your marriage has been difficult.
And slowly, quietly, the heart that once delighted in what God gave begins craving what God has forbidden.
The scandal rarely begins in a hotel room.
Sometimes it begins with attention.
Someone noticed you.
Someone laughed at your joke.
Someone listened to what your spouse seemed too exhausted to hear.
Someone made you feel attractive again.
Someone made you feel important again.
And you told yourself:
We’re only talking.
That sentence has buried more boundaries than many people would ever admit.
Scripture understands the human heart better than we do.
That is why Proverbs does not merely say, “Do not commit adultery.”
It redirects desire.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
There is something profoundly beautiful here.
God is not embarrassed by covenant desire.
He created the body.
He created affection.
He created attraction.
He created marriage.
Before pornography corrupted desire…
before adultery weaponized desire…
before lust detached desire from love…
before shame convinced people that physical intimacy itself must somehow be dirty…
God looked upon the man and woman He had created and declared His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:31).
Sin did not invent sexuality.
God did.
Sin distorted it.
And redemption does not require us to call God’s good creation evil.
Redemption teaches us to receive God’s gifts according to God’s design.
That is why the Song of Songs can speak about marital and romantic desire with language that is poetic, physical, tender, and intense.
Song of Songs 5:1 contains another extraordinary expression:
שְׁתוּ וְשִׁכְרוּ דּוֹדִים
shethu veshikhru dodim.
“Drink, yea, drink abundantly, O beloved.”

Translations differ over exactly how to express the final wording and who is being addressed, but the imagery is unmistakably celebratory. The Hebrew verb שָׁכַר (shakar) is associated with becoming drunk or intoxicated, while the poetic context celebrates love rather than condemning drunken excess.
Again, Scripture takes the imagery of abundance and overwhelming delight and places it within a celebration of love.
Why?
Because biblical holiness is not emotional anesthesia.
God does not save human beings by turning them into creatures who feel nothing.
He teaches us what to love.
He teaches us how to love.
He teaches us where desire belongs.
That distinction matters.
The Bible condemns drunkenness precisely because intoxication can surrender the faculties that should remain under righteous control.
Ephesians 5:18 says:
“And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit.”
The Greek begins:
καὶ μὴ μεθύσκεσθε οἴνῳ
kai mē methyskesthe oinō
“And do not become drunk with wine…”
Then Paul gives the contrast:
ἀλλὰ πληροῦσθε ἐν πνεύματι
alla plērousthe en pneumati
“…but be filled with the Spirit.”
So Scripture is not confused.
It does not condemn drunkenness in one place and secretly endorse it somewhere else.
The Bible can use intoxication metaphorically because metaphors borrow a recognizable feature of something without endorsing every feature of the comparison.
When someone says, “I was drunk with happiness,” they are not necessarily saying they consumed alcohol.
They mean the happiness was overwhelming.
Likewise, the language of Proverbs communicates something powerful:
Let covenant love have your attention.
Treasure your spouse.
Return to her.
Return to him.
Cultivate delight instead of feeding fantasies about someone else.
And that may be where this becomes painful.
Because someone reading this remembers what marriage used to feel like.
You remember talking until two in the morning.
You remember waiting for their message.
You remember how your stomach felt when you saw their name appear on your phone.
You remember the wedding.
You remember the promises.
You remember believing nothing could separate you.
Then came bills.
Children.
Stress.
Work.
Exhaustion.
Disappointments.
Arguments that were never completely resolved.
Words that cannot be pulled back into the mouth once spoken.
Silences that lasted too long.
Beds where two bodies were inches apart while two hearts felt miles away.
Maybe nobody cheated.
But something disappeared.
And now you are reading a command to “rejoice with the wife of thy youth,” and instead of inspiration you feel grief.
Because you want to ask:
What if the delight is gone?
That is where shallow Christianity often gives shallow answers.
“Just pray harder.”
“Go on a date.”
“Be more romantic.”
Sometimes those things help.
Sometimes the wounds go deeper.
Betrayal can be real.
Neglect can be real.
Abuse can be real.
Trauma can be real.
Broken trust can be real.
And Scripture never requires someone to pretend evil is harmless in order to appear spiritual.
Forgiveness is not calling darkness light.
Grace is not pretending betrayal did not hurt.
Reconciliation, where possible, involves truth.
Repentance involves truth.
Healing involves truth.
The cross itself proves that God does not heal sin by pretending sin is insignificant.
Look at Calvary.
If sin were insignificant, there would have been no cross.
Jesus Christ did not bleed because our rebellion was trivial.
He bled because our rebellion was deadly.
And He loved us anyway.
That is the shocking center of Christianity.
Not that decent people occasionally make mistakes and God politely overlooks them.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves were pursued by a holy God.
“For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.”
Romans 5:6.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired ourselves.
Not after we finally deserved Him.
Christ died for the ungodly.
And suddenly the theme of covenant becomes even larger.
Marriage is precious, but marriage is not the Savior.
Your husband cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
Your wife cannot carry the weight of being your Messiah.
Romance cannot save your soul.
Sex cannot heal the deepest separation between humanity and God.
Being desired cannot give you eternal life.
Only Jesus can.
And sometimes our relationships begin collapsing under expectations no human being was created to carry.
We ask another sinner:
Make me whole.
Never disappoint me.
Always understand me.
Make me feel valuable.
Make me feel beautiful.
Make me feel wanted.
Never change.
Never fail.
Never leave me emotionally hungry.
Then another imperfect human being inevitably fails to become God for us.
And resentment grows.
Christian marriage becomes healthier when Christ returns to the center because both husband and wife can finally stop demanding salvation from each other.
Jesus is Savior.
Your spouse is your spouse.
And because Christ is Savior, you can begin learning how to love another imperfect person without pretending imperfection is righteousness.
This is where Proverbs 5 becomes far more profound than “have a passionate marriage.”
It is teaching covenant loyalty in a world of counterfeit pleasures.
The forbidden woman offers something.
The covenant wife represents something else.
One path says:
Take what feels good now.
The other says:
Cherish what you promised before God.
One whispers:
Nobody will know.
Covenant asks:
Who are you becoming?
One says:
You deserve this.
Wisdom asks:
Where does this road end?
That question could save someone reading this today.
Where does this road end?
Not:
How exciting does it feel tonight?
Not:
How much attention am I receiving?
Not:
Can I hide it?
Where does this road end?
Proverbs 5 forces us to look past the first taste toward the final consequence.
Because temptation loves editing.
It shows you the kiss but cuts out the confession.
It shows you the excitement but cuts out the devastated spouse.
It shows you the fantasy but cuts out the children asking why everything changed.
It shows you the secret message but cuts out the moment the phone is discovered.
It shows you pleasure without consequence.
Scripture restores the missing scenes.
And then Scripture does something even more beautiful.
It points you home.
“Rejoice with the wife of thy youth.”
Maybe somebody needs those words before doing something they will spend years wishing they could undo.
Go home.
Not merely to your address.
Go home in your heart.
Turn away from the fantasy.
Delete what needs to be deleted.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
End the conversation that has crossed boundaries.
Stop feeding the secret life.
Ask for help.
Seek wise pastoral counsel.
Seek qualified professional help when the situation requires it.
Do not keep walking toward the cliff because turning around feels embarrassing.
Repentance is not humiliation for humiliation’s sake.
Repentance is turning.
The New Testament word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια (metanoia), carrying the idea of a changed mind, a reorientation that produces a changed direction.
Jesus did not come merely to make sinners feel terrible about where they have been.
He came to call sinners out of death and into life.
Maybe your scandal is adultery.
Maybe pornography.
Maybe emotional infidelity.
Maybe years of bitterness.
Maybe you stopped touching your spouse because resentment became safer than vulnerability.
Maybe you have been comparing the person beside you with carefully edited strangers on a screen.
Maybe your spouse does not know how lonely you have become.
Maybe your marriage looks beautiful on Facebook and feels empty behind the front door.
Maybe you are unmarried and this exposes the way you have been treating other people’s bodies as entertainment.
Maybe you are the betrayed spouse and reading about marital delight hurts because somebody else shattered what you guarded.
Or maybe your deepest scandal has nothing to do with marriage.
You simply know what it is like to want something God has said cannot give you life.
Then hear this carefully.
Your worst chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
That is not because consequences magically disappear.
It is because Jesus Christ specializes in resurrecting what sin declares finished.
Peter denied Him.
Thomas doubted.
Paul persecuted Christians.
The Samaritan woman carried a complicated relational history.
The woman caught in adultery stood publicly exposed.
Again and again, Scripture introduces us to human beings whose stories contain things they would probably have preferred erased.
Jesus did not pretend sin was righteousness.
Neither did He reduce people to their sin.
Grace tells the truth and then opens a door.
Christ’s words to the woman caught in adultery capture both realities:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.”
Grace.
And transformation.
Forgiveness.
And a new direction.
No condemnation from Christ for the repentant sinner does not mean sin suddenly becomes harmless.
It means sin no longer gets to be the sinner’s master.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
By refusing to let the scandal have the final word.
And perhaps now we can understand why Scripture dares to speak so intensely about marital love.
God is not ashamed of holy affection.
He is protecting it.
He knows counterfeit intimacy can destroy real intimacy.
He knows lust consumes people while covenant learns to cherish them.
Pornography trains the eyes to consume.
Adultery takes what covenant has not given.
Selfishness asks, “What can you do for me?”
Covenant asks, “How can I faithfully love you before God?”
And biblical marital intimacy belongs inside that larger reality of knowing, giving, faithfulness, tenderness, exclusivity, sacrifice, delight, and covenant.
This does not mean every Christian marriage will feel emotionally intoxicating every day.
Proverbs is wisdom literature, not a promise that spouses will permanently experience romantic euphoria.
There will be ordinary Tuesdays.
There will be sickness.
There will be aging.
There will be exhaustion.
There may be seasons when intimacy requires patience, communication, medical care, counseling, repentance, rebuilding trust, or simply learning to be tender again.
Biblical love is deeper than adrenaline.
The command to rejoice in your spouse does not mean manufacturing a permanent emotional high.
It means refusing to treat covenant love as disposable simply because novelty has faded.
Sometimes mature love looks less like fireworks and more like someone sitting beside a hospital bed at 3:17 in the morning.
Sometimes “intoxicated with her love” eventually looks like wrinkled hands still reaching for each other after fifty years.
Sometimes passion becomes patience.
Sometimes attraction becomes admiration.
Sometimes romance becomes endurance.
Sometimes love becomes the quiet sentence:
I am still here.
And perhaps that is more beautiful than the first rush ever was.
Because anyone can become fascinated by novelty.
Covenant learns to rediscover wonder in someone familiar.
That is difficult.
It is also sacred.
And there is an even greater love behind every faithful human covenant.
Jesus.
The Bridegroom who did not abandon His people when they became difficult to love.
The Savior who knew exactly what our sin would cost Him and walked toward the cross anyway.
The King who was betrayed, mocked, stripped, beaten, pierced, and crucified—and who rose again.
Christianity is not ultimately the story of humanity desperately climbing toward God.
It is the story of God coming for sinners.
That is why the answer to corrupted desire cannot merely be “try harder.”
We need new hearts.
We need grace.
We need the Holy Spirit.
We need Christ.
We need forgiveness when we fall and strength to walk differently when we rise.
And perhaps somebody has reached this sentence carrying a secret.
Nobody around you knows.
Your spouse does not know.
Your church does not know.
Your family does not know.
But God knows.
And you expected that sentence to terrify you.
Maybe it should sober you.
But it should also give you hope.
Because the God who knows the chapter you hide is the same God who sent His Son to save sinners.
Stop running.
Come into the light.
Not because exposure is painless.
Because darkness cannot heal what it is allowed to keep.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Notice who is faithful.
He is.
When you have been faithless, He remains who He is.
When you have wandered, Christ still calls sinners to return.
When you have polluted something God intended to be beautiful, grace can begin the painful, holy work of restoration.

And when restoration of a particular human relationship is complicated or not possible, Christ Himself remains sufficient. The Gospel is larger than a marital status and larger than a relationship outcome.
So no, Scripture is not giving Christians permission to become drunk.
It is giving married people a picture of covenant delight so consuming that forbidden counterfeits should lose their throne.
Be captivated by faithful love.
Protect it.
Cultivate it.
Thank God for it.
And above everything else, be captured by the greater love to which every Christian marriage ultimately points:
the love of Christ.
Be honest.
Not because every sentence will be comfortable, but because there may come a night when temptation makes you forget what daylight taught you.
Someone may be sitting beside a spouse tonight while silently wondering whether their marriage is worth fighting for.
Someone may believe sexual sin has placed them beyond the reach of Christ.
Let this reach them.
And even send it to the person who does not believe in Jesus yet.
Because beneath this discussion about marriage is a much greater announcement:
There is a Savior for sinners.
It does not.
Not because supporting Gospel Warrior is a requirement for salvation.
It is not.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by purchasing access to a ministry.
And not because anyone should be manipulated into giving by being told that God will love them more if they pay.
The Gospel allows no such bargain.
But if this ministry genuinely helps you grow in Christ, supporting it can be one practical, voluntary way of helping biblical content continue reaching people who need it.

Your support helps us keep writing, teaching, sharing, and building resources intended to point people toward Jesus. Sharing this article costs nothing, yet it can carry the Gospel into a home we could never personally enter.
Jesus does not need another customer.
He calls disciples.
He calls sinners to repent.
He calls the weary to come.
He calls the hidden into the light.
He calls the forgiven into holiness.
He calls husbands to faithfulness.
He calls wives to faithfulness.
He calls the unmarried to purity.
He calls His people away from counterfeit intoxications and toward something infinitely greater:
Himself.
So go back to the question.
Why does Scripture compare marital love to intoxication?
Because God understands how powerfully the human heart can become captivated.
And instead of pretending desire does not exist, biblical wisdom asks where that desire will lead you.
Toward consumption or covenant?
Toward secrecy or truth?
Toward betrayal or faithfulness?
Toward a counterfeit that promises life and quietly steals it…
or toward the wisdom of the God who created love in the first place?
Maybe tonight the greatest miracle will not be that you suddenly feel something spectacular.
Maybe it will be simpler.
You put the phone down.
You close the secret conversation.
You confess.
You pray.
You reach across the bed.
You ask forgiveness.
You choose faithfulness again.
You ask Jesus to teach your heart how to love what is holy.
And somewhere between the scandal you cannot undo and the grace you could never earn, you discover the truth that has rescued sinners for two thousand years:
Jesus is still writing.
